title: Compounds of Carbon Containing Halogens (Haloalkanes and Haloarenes)
summary: Haloalkanes (R–X) have the halogen on an sp³ carbon and are primary, secondary or tertiary; haloarenes (Ar–X) have halogen on an sp² carbon of an aromatic ring; allylic and benzylic halides have halogen on the carbon next to a double bond or a benzene ring; vinylic halides have halogen on an sp² carbon of a C=C. Preparation of haloalkanes: from alcohols (R–OH + SOCl2 → R–Cl + SO2 + HCl is the best method; HX with ZnCl2; PCl5, PCl3/P + I2), from alkanes (free-radical halogenation, gives mixtures), from alkenes (HX addition, Markovnikov's rule), halogen exchange (Finkelstein reaction: R–Cl + NaI in acetone → R–I; Swarts: R–Cl + AgF → R–F). Haloarenes: electrophilic halogenation of benzene (Cl2/FeCl3), Sandmeyer reaction (ArN2+Cl− with CuCl or CuBr) and Gattermann reaction (Cu powder + HX). Boiling points rise with molecular mass and fall with branching: RI > RBr > RCl > RF; haloalkanes are insoluble in water but dissolve in organic solvents.

Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution: SN2 (one step, inversion of configuration, rate = k[RX][Nu], favoured by primary halides and polar aprotic solvent: CH3X > 1° > 2°) and SN1 (two steps via a carbocation, racemisation, rate = k[RX], favoured by tertiary halides and polar protic solvents: 3° > 2° > 1°). Reactions: with aq. KOH → alcohol; alc. KOH → alkene (elimination, Saytzeff); KCN → nitrile; AgCN → isonitrile; NH3 → amine; Na/dry ether (Wurtz); Mg/dry ether → Grignard reagent RMgX (a strong nucleophile and base; with H2O gives alkane: RMgX + H2O → R–H + Mg(OH)X; with CO2 gives carboxylic acid; with HCHO gives a primary alcohol, with other aldehydes secondary alcohol and with ketones tertiary alcohol). Haloarenes are much less reactive in nucleophilic substitution than haloalkanes because: the C–X bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance, the carbon is sp² (shorter, stronger bond) and the phenyl cation is unstable; nitro groups at the ortho/para positions make substitution easier. Haloarenes undergo electrophilic substitution (o,p-directing but deactivating) and Wurtz–Fittig and Fittig reactions.

Dichloromethane (solvent, paint remover), chloroform (CHCl3, anaesthetic earlier; oxidises in air to poisonous phosgene COCl2, so it is stored in dark bottles filled to the brim), iodoform (CHI3, antiseptic), carbon tetrachloride (fire extinguisher, now banned: ozone depletion), freons or CFCs (refrigerants; deplete the ozone layer) and DDT (insecticide, non-biodegradable, accumulates in the food chain). Chloroform with a base and primary amine gives the isocyanide test (carbylamine).

objective: (a) What is a Grignard reagent? (b) Write the reaction of CH3MgBr with water.
(a) An organomagnesium halide, RMgX, prepared from RX and Mg in dry ether. (b) CH3MgBr + H2O → CH4 + Mg(OH)Br.

vsa: What is a Grignard reagent? How is it prepared?
An organomagnesium halide, R–Mg–X. It is prepared by reacting an alkyl or aryl halide with magnesium metal in dry ether: R–X + Mg → RMgX.
Why is chlorobenzene less reactive than chloroethane in nucleophilic substitution?
In chlorobenzene the C–Cl bond has a partial double-bond character due to resonance, and the carbon is sp² hybridised (shorter, stronger bond); in addition, the phenyl cation is unstable.
Distinguish between SN1 and SN2 reactions (two points).

SN1: two steps through a carbocation, rate depends on [RX] only, racemisation, tertiary halides favoured. SN2: single step, rate depends on [RX][Nu], inversion of configuration, primary halides favoured.
How is chloroform stored and why?
In dark brown bottles filled to the brim because light and air oxidise it to poisonous phosgene gas, COCl2; about 1% ethanol is added to convert phosgene to harmless ethyl carbonate.
Write the Sandmeyer reaction for the preparation of chlorobenzene from benzene diazonium chloride.
What is the Finkelstein reaction? Write an example.
Conversion of alkyl chlorides or bromides to iodides with NaI in dry acetone: CH3CH2Br + NaI → CH3CH2I + NaBr (NaBr precipitates).
Why are haloalkanes insoluble in water though polar?
The energy released on forming new haloalkane–water attraction is less than that needed to break the hydrogen bonds of water and the dipole–dipole attractions of the haloalkane.
Name two harmful effects of freons and DDT.
Freons deplete the ozone layer (cause skin cancer); DDT is non-biodegradable and accumulates in the food chain, harming birds and aquatic life.
sa: Explain the mechanism of the SN2 reaction of CH3Br with OH−.

The nucleophile OH− attacks the carbon from the side opposite to Br (backside) in a single step through a transition state in which C is partly bonded to both OH and Br; Br− leaves and the configuration is inverted; rate = k[CH3Br][OH−].
Write the reactions of a Grignard reagent with (a) CO2 (b) methanal (c) a ketone.
(a) RMgX + CO2 → RCOOMgX → RCOOH (carboxylic acid). (b) RMgX + HCHO → RCH2OMgX → RCH2OH (primary alcohol). (c) RMgX + R'COR' → R3COMgX → tertiary alcohol after hydrolysis.
How will you prepare (a) ethyl iodide from ethanol (b) chlorobenzene from aniline (c) 2-chloropropane from propene?

(a) C2H5OH + SOCl2 → C2H5Cl, then NaI/acetone gives C2H5I (or red P + I2). (b) Aniline → diazotisation (NaNO2/HCl, 273 K) → C6H5N2+Cl− → CuCl (Sandmeyer). (c) CH3CH=CH2 + HCl → CH3CHClCH3 (Markovnikov).
Give reasons: (a) SN1 reactions are favoured by tertiary halides. (b) Haloalkanes have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar mass.
(a) The tertiary carbocation is stabilised by three alkyl groups (+I and hyperconjugation). (b) Haloalkanes are polar with dipole–dipole attractions and greater van der Waals forces than alkanes.
Compare haloalkanes and haloarenes in respect of nucleophilic substitution, bond length of C–X and dipole moment.

Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution readily (C–X longer, 177 pm in CH3Cl, higher dipole moment 1.85 D); haloarenes resist it (C–X shorter, 169 pm in C6H5Cl, because of resonance and sp² carbon, lower dipole moment 1.69 D).
Write short notes on chloroform and iodoform: preparation and uses.

Chloroform: ethanol/acetone with bleaching powder (haloform reaction), CH3CH2OH → CHCl3; solvent and used for making freon. Iodoform: ethanol + I2 + NaOH, CHI3 (yellow solid); used as an antiseptic for dressing wounds.
la: (a) Explain halogenation of alkanes and write the mechanism briefly. (b) Compare haloalkanes and haloarenes with respect to nucleophilic substitution and give reasons. (c) Write the uses of methanol-derived and halogen compounds (CCl4, CHCl3).

(a) Alkanes react with Cl2 in sunlight by a free-radical chain mechanism giving a mixture of haloalkanes: initiation (Cl2 → 2Cl•), propagation (Cl• + RH → R• + HCl; R• + Cl2 → RCl + Cl•), termination (radical coupling).
(b) Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) readily; haloarenes do not because of the resonance partial double bond, sp² C–X, and repulsion of the nucleophile by the π cloud; nitro groups at o/p positions activate.
(c) CCl4: dry cleaning and fire extinguishers; CHCl3: solvent, preparation of freon and former anaesthetic.
(a) Give the preparation of haloalkanes from alcohols, alkenes and halogen exchange. (b) Write the products of RX with aq. KOH, alc. KOH, KCN and AgCN.

(a) From alcohols: R–OH + SOCl2 → RCl + SO2 + HCl; from alkenes: addition of HX (Markovnikov); halogen exchange: Finkelstein (RCl + NaI → RI) and Swarts (RCl + AgF → RF).
(b) aq. KOH → R–OH; alc. KOH → alkene; KCN → R–CN (nitrile); AgCN → R–NC (isocyanide).
(a) Discuss SN1 and SN2 mechanisms with stereochemistry. (b) Predict the order of reactivity of CH3Br, CH3CH2Br, (CH3)2CHBr, (CH3)3CBr in SN2 and SN1.

(a) SN2: backside attack, concerted, inversion (Walden), rate = k[RX][Nu]. SN1: ionisation to a planar carbocation then attack on either face, racemisation of an optically active halide, rate = k[RX].
(b) SN2: CH3Br > CH3CH2Br > (CH3)2CHBr > (CH3)3CBr (steric hindrance). SN1: (CH3)3CBr > (CH3)2CHBr > CH3CH2Br > CH3Br (carbocation stability).
(a) Describe the Sandmeyer and Gattermann reactions and the Wurtz–Fittig reaction with equations. (b) State the environmental effects of CFCs and DDT.

(a) Sandmeyer: ArN2+Cl− + CuCl → ArCl + N2 (similarly CuBr). Gattermann: ArN2+X− + Cu/HX → ArX. Wurtz–Fittig: ArX + RX + 2Na → Ar–R + 2NaX (dry ether).
(b) CFCs release Cl atoms in the stratosphere that destroy ozone; DDT does not degrade, accumulates in fatty tissue and food chains and reduces the eggshell thickness of birds.
